paraphrase: After his father's death his relatives seized the family's wealth; at his mother's urging Milarepa learned sorcery, caused a house to collapse at a wedding feast killing thirty-five people, and destroyed the villagers' harvest with hail; seized by remorse, he resolved to seek the Dharma.
notes: Reference from memory; the text is not available locally. The 'black deeds'; numbers follow Tsangnyön Heruka's version.

paraphrase: Marpa made Milarepa build towers and tear them down again, beat and humiliated him, and withheld initiation, so as to purify the karma of his evil deeds; Milarepa's despair and Marpa's later explanation that each ordeal cleansed a great sin.
notes: Reference from memory; the text is not available locally.

paraphrase: Dagmema, pitying Milarepa, sent him to Ngok Chöku Dorje with a forged letter; Ngok taught him, but no experience arose; when the deception came out Marpa showed that instruction given without the root guru's consent could not bear fruit.
notes: Reference from memory; the text is not available locally.

paraphrase: After empowerment Milarepa meditated alone in caves for years, wearing a single cotton cloth, sustained by inner heat and living on nettles until his body turned green; he gained realization through Marpa's instructions of inner heat and Mahāmudrā.
notes: Reference from memory; the text is not available locally.

paraphrase: At Gampopa's departure Milarepa said he had one last, most profound instruction and, lifting his robe, showed his seat calloused hard as horn from years of sitting: that is the instruction — meditate with such perseverance.
notes: Reference from memory; the text is not available locally. Some versions set this episode differently; moderate.

paraphrase: Milarepa, poisoned by a jealous scholar's concubine, knew it and accepted it; at his death miraculous signs appeared and the ḍākinīs took his relics.

paraphrase: Marpa foretold that Milarepa, through his faith and effort, would attain buddhahood in one life and one body, as he did by the tradition's account.
